Fireworks AI's own listing describes it as Alibaba's latest flagship closed model, available exclusively through Fireworks outside of Alibaba's own infrastructure, and shows function-calling (tool use) support. Alibaba does not publish parameter counts, architecture details or benchmark scores for this closed model on the pages available.
disadvantages: Closed, proprietary model: Alibaba does not publish parameter counts, architecture details (dense or Mixture-of-Experts) or independently verifiable benchmark scores for it on the pages available.

fireworks_ai-embedding-models/fireworks_.description: Qwen3.8-Max (served on Fireworks AI as "qwen3p8-max") is Qwen's flagship large language model, released as the open-weight checkpoint Qwen/Qwen3.8-2.4T-A95B: a Mixture-of-Experts model with 2.4 trillion total parameters and 95 billion activated per token, built on the architectural foundation of Qwen3.5. The model card calls it "the most capable generation in the Qwen open-model family to date" and the first time a Qwen-Max-class model has been given an open release, aimed at coding, professional work, research, and long-horizon agentic tasks. Reasoning depth can be tuned with a reasoning_effort setting, and image input is available through Qwen's hosted Qwen3.8-Max product tier, which is what Fireworks serves.
disadvantages: Fine-tuning is not supported on Fireworks' serverless offering of this model, per Fireworks AI's model page.
The open-weight checkpoint itself is text-only; vision input is documented as a feature of Qwen's separately hosted Qwen3.8-Max product tier, not the raw checkpoint, per the model card.

gemini/gemini-flash-latest.description: gemini-flash-latest is Google's rolling alias for the current release of its Gemini Flash-tier model on the Gemini Developer API, rather than a fixed, dated model. Google's Gemini API documentation describes a 'latest' name as pointing 'to the latest release for a specific model variation', an alias that 'will get hot-swapped with every new release of a specific model variation'; Google gives at least two weeks' email notice before a breaking change to the model behind the alias. As of 24 September 2026, Google's Gemini API models page lists Gemini 3.8 Flash as the newest stable Flash-tier release, though Google does not publish an explicit statement that the alias currently names that exact snapshot.
disadvantages: Because the alias is hot-swapped with each new release, the exact underlying model version, and its behavior and benchmark scores, can change without any corresponding change to application code, per Google's Gemini API documentation.
Google's own naming-convention guidance recommends most production apps use a specific stable model string rather than a rolling alias like this one.

use_cases: Cost-sensitive, non-time-sensitive transcription of long audio files stored in Cloud Storage

advantages: Clones a voice from as little as up to 10 seconds of reference audio, according to Google's documentation.
Supports 25 languages, including multiple English and French locale variants, German, Chinese, Japanese, Korean, Arabic, Russian and several Indian regional languages, per Google's documentation.
Multilingual transfer lets an en-US voice cloning key synthesize speech in German, Spanish, French and Portuguese.
Supports text-based prompting, pace control from 0.25x to 2x speed, pause tags, and custom pronunciation via phonetic encoding.
google_speech/instant-custom-voice.description: Chirp 3: Instant Custom Voice is a Google Cloud Text-to-Speech feature that clones a voice from a short audio sample and lets that cloned voice be used to synthesize new speech from text. Google's documentation describes providing up to 10 seconds of clean, single-channel consent and reference audio, from which the service generates a text-string 'voice cloning key' that can later be used to synthesize speech. Access is restricted to allow-listed users, who must contact Google's sales team.
disadvantages: Access is restricted to allow-listed users and requires contacting Google's sales team, rather than being generally available.
Reference audio must be close to 10 seconds with no background noise, limiting usable source recordings.
use_cases: Personalized audio content creation from a cloned voice
Multilingual voice synthesis from a single voice sample

advantages: Automatically detects and labels which speaker (provider or patient) said each part of the transcript, per Google's documentation.
Supports automatic punctuation, alternate transcriptions, word timestamps and word-level confidence scores.
google_speech/medical-conversation.description: The medical_conversation model is a Google Cloud Speech-to-Text V1 model tailored for transcribing dialogue between a medical provider, such as a doctor or nurse, and a patient. Google's documentation states words spoken by each speaker are automatically detected and labeled in the returned transcript, and the model is available only for en-US audio. Google's Speech-to-Text V1 docs recommend that new users use the V2 API instead, though medical_conversation is a V1-specific model.
disadvantages: Only available for en-US audio, per Google's documentation.
Is a Speech-to-Text V1 model; Google's documentation recommends new Speech-to-Text users use the V2 API instead.
use_cases: Transcribing conversations between a medical provider and a patient, such as clinical visits

advantages: Recognizes medical vocabulary — diagnoses, medications, symptoms, treatments, and conditions — that Google's general-purpose Speech-to-Text models are not tuned for.
Automatically enables spoken punctuation, formatting commands, and spoken headings, features Google's documentation says "cannot be disabled" for this model.

Supports automatic punctuation (enabled by default), alternate transcriptions, word timestamps, and word-level confidence, the only additional features Google's documentation allows with medical models.
google_speech/medical-dictation.description: Medical Dictation is one of Google Cloud Speech-to-Text's two medical speech recognition models, alongside Medical Conversation, tuned for notes dictated by a single medical provider — for example, a doctor dictating notes about a patient's blood test results — and for vocabulary such as diagnoses, medications, symptoms, treatments, and conditions. It is offered through Speech-to-Text's v1 API and, per Google's documentation, is available only for US English.
disadvantages: Available only for US English (en-US); Google's documentation states medical models are not offered in any other language.
Listed only among Speech-to-Text's v1 API models; it does not appear among the v2 API's Chirp-based models (chirp_3, chirp_2, telephony) in Google's current documentation.
use_cases: Transcribing a single medical provider's dictated notes, such as a doctor recording findings from a patient's blood test.
Capturing medical documentation with correctly recognized diagnosis, medication, symptom, treatment, and condition terminology.
Structured dictation workflows that rely on spoken punctuation, spoken headings, and formatting commands to shape the transcript.

advantages: Built on the same neural technology Google uses to create a Custom Voice, giving custom-voice-level naturalness without training a bespoke voice model, per Google's documentation.
Covers 17 languages and locales, including English, French, Spanish, German, Danish, Italian, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, Hindi, Thai, and Vietnamese, per Google's current supported-voices table.
US English alone offers 9 distinct Neural2 voices and UK English 7, spanning multiple male and female options, per Google's voice list.
google_speech/neural2.description: Neural2 is a text-to-speech voice type offered by Google Cloud Text-to-Speech, built, per Google's documentation, on "the same technology used to create a Custom Voice," giving custom-voice-level naturalness without training and submitting a customer's own recordings. As of Google's current supported-voices table it spans 17 languages and locales — English (US, UK, Australian, and Indian), French (France and Canadian), Spanish (Spain and US), German, Danish, Italian, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese (Brazilian), Hindi, Thai, and Vietnamese — with between 1 and 9 voices per locale. Google's current voice-type documentation does not mark Neural2 as deprecated or legacy.

sources.title: Supported voices and languages | Cloud Text-to-Speech

use_cases: Natural-sounding narration and IVR or voice-assistant prompts in a supported language without training a custom voice model.
Multilingual applications needing English, French, or Spanish locale variants, plus German, Danish, Italian, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, Hindi, Thai, or Vietnamese, within one TTS tier.
Applications wanting a choice among several male and female voices per locale, such as the nine US English Neural2 voices.

advantages: Remains listed as an active, non-deprecated voice type in Google's current Text-to-Speech voice-type documentation.
Available in six locales — Australian English, US English, French, German, and Spanish (Spain and US) — each with a dedicated Polyglot-1 voice, per Google's voice list.
google_speech/polyglot.description: Polyglot is one of the voice types offered by Google Cloud Text-to-Speech, listed alongside Standard, WaveNet, Neural2, Studio, and Chirp 3: HD voices in Google's own voice-type documentation. As of Google's current voice list it comprises six voices — en-AU-Polyglot-1, en-US-Polyglot-1, fr-FR-Polyglot-1, de-DE-Polyglot-1, es-ES-Polyglot-1, and es-US-Polyglot-1, all male — making it Google's smallest TTS voice type by language and voice coverage. Google's documentation does not mark Polyglot as deprecated or legacy, but also does not publish a dedicated description of its underlying technology or intended use case.
disadvantages: Limited to six voices (en-AU-Polyglot-1, en-US-Polyglot-1, fr-FR-Polyglot-1, de-DE-Polyglot-1, es-ES-Polyglot-1, es-US-Polyglot-1), all male, far fewer than Google's Standard, WaveNet, or Neural2 tiers.
Google's documentation does not publish a dedicated description of Polyglot's underlying technology or recommended use case, unlike its Neural2, Studio, and Chirp 3: HD voice types.

sources.title: Supported voices and languages | Cloud Text-to-Speech

use_cases: General-purpose text-to-speech output in Australian English, US English, French, German, or Spanish (Spain or US) where a male Polyglot voice is wanted.
Applications already using Google Cloud Text-to-Speech that want an additional male voice option in one of these six locales.

advantages: Provides access to discounted pricing on Cloud Speech-to-Text transcription in exchange for allowing Google to log the submitted audio and transcripts, per Google's Data Logging documentation.
Speech-to-Text API includes recognition features such as automatic punctuation and word-level confidence, per Google's Speech-to-Text documentation.
google_speech/speech-recognition-with-da.description: This is Google Cloud Speech-to-Text's V1 API transcription service used with Google's opt-in data logging program enabled. Customers who opt a project into data logging allow Google to use the audio and transcripts it submits to refine and improve Cloud Speech-to-Text's service quality, and in exchange gain access to discounted pricing, per Google's Data Logging documentation. By default, Cloud Speech-to-Text does not log customer audio data or transcripts; logging only happens once a project explicitly opts in.
disadvantages: Audio and transcripts logged under this program are not deleted when the project is deleted; removal requires submitting a separate deletion request form, per Google's Data Logging documentation.
Only a limited set of authorized Google employees and contractors have access to the logged customer data, per Google's Data Logging documentation.
use_cases: Transcribing spoken audio to text via the Speech-to-Text V1 API for customers willing to let Google log audio and transcripts in exchange for discounted transcription pricing, per Google's Data Logging documentation.

advantages: Audio and transcripts are not logged by Google, since data logging is off by default on Cloud Speech-to-Text, per Google's Data Logging documentation.
Speech-to-Text API includes recognition features such as automatic punctuation and word-level confidence, per Google's Speech-to-Text documentation.
google_speech/speech-recognition-without.description: This is Google Cloud Speech-to-Text's V1 API transcription service in its default configuration, with Google's opt-in data logging program not enabled. By default, Cloud Speech-to-Text does not log customer audio data or transcripts, per Google's Data Logging documentation; a project only has its audio and transcripts logged if it explicitly opts into the data logging program, which this configuration has not done. Data sent to a project without data logging enabled is used by Google only as needed to provide the service, not to refine or improve its products, per Google's Data Logging documentation.
disadvantages: Does not receive the discounted pricing that Google offers to projects that opt into the data logging program, per Google's Data Logging documentation.
use_cases: Transcribing spoken audio to text via the Speech-to-Text V1 API for customers who do not want their audio or transcripts logged by Google, per Google's Data Logging documentation.

advantages: Offered across dozens of languages and locale variants, per Google's supported voices and languages table.
Supports SSML markup to control pronunciation, pacing and pitch, and is listed as a generally available (GA) voice tier.
Can output audio as MP3 or LINEAR16 (WAV), for use in applications or to augment media such as videos and audio recordings.
google_speech/standard.description: Google Cloud Text-to-Speech's Standard voices are the entry tier of Google's Cloud Text-to-Speech API. Many Standard voices use a variation of parametric text-to-speech technology, which Google describes as generating audio by passing output through vocoder-based signal processing. They sit alongside Google's newer WaveNet, Neural2, Studio and Chirp voice tiers; Google says WaveNet voices, for example, are built from models 'trained using raw audio samples of actual humans speaking.' Standard voices are offered across dozens of languages and locale variants in Google's supported voices table, remain generally available (GA), and support SSML markup for controlling pronunciation and pacing.
disadvantages: Many Standard voices use older parametric, vocoder-based synthesis; Google says its WaveNet-generated voices sound 'more warm and human-like' than other synthetic voices such as Standard.
Does not support real-time bidirectional streaming synthesis; among Cloud TTS voice tiers, only Chirp 3: HD voices offer that, per Google's voice type overview table.

sources.title: Supported voices and languages | Cloud Text-to-Speech | Google Cloud Documentation
Cloud Text-to-Speech basics | Google Cloud Documentation

use_cases: Powering voice assistant apps that give users natural-language spoken feedback, such as confirming a completed action.
Augmenting media such as videos or audio recordings with spoken narration.
General-purpose text-to-speech for applications that play back human speech to users.

advantages: Reached general availability (GA) as a voice type purpose-built for news reading and broadcast content, per Google's Voice Types documentation and February 2024 release notes.
Designed specifically for long-form texts such as narration and news reading, per Google's Text-to-Speech release notes.
Supports SSML markup for controlling speech output, per Google's Voice Types documentation.
google_speech/studio.description: Studio voices are a Google Cloud Text-to-Speech voice type designed for news reading and broadcast content, and are intended for use with long-form texts such as narration and news reading, per Google's Voice Types and release-note documentation. They reached general availability in February 2024. Google's Voices list documents Studio voices for English (UK), English (US), and French (France), with named voices such as en-GB-Studio-B and fr-FR-Studio-A; a related Studio multispeaker voice type for discussions and interviews remains experimental.
disadvantages: Documented for only three languages/locales (English UK, English US, and French France), per Google's Voices documentation, far fewer than Google's Standard or WaveNet voice types.
Does not support the <mark>, <emphasis>, <prosody pitch>, or <lang> SSML tags that other voice types allow, per Google's Voice Types documentation.

sources.title: Supported voices and languages | Cloud Text-to-Speech Documentation

use_cases: News reading and broadcast-style content, per Google's Voice Types documentation.
Long-form narration, per Google's Text-to-Speech release notes.

advantages: Trained on raw audio samples of real human speech, producing more human-like emphasis and inflection on syllables, phonemes and words than other synthetic voices, per Google's Voice Types documentation.
Offered across dozens of languages and regional variants, including Arabic, Bengali, Czech, Danish, Dutch, English, Filipino, Finnish, and French, per Google's Voices documentation.
google_speech/wavenet.description: WaveNet voices are a premium Google Cloud Text-to-Speech voice type built from models trained on raw audio samples of actual humans speaking, which Google's documentation says lets them generate synthetic speech with more human-like emphasis and inflection on syllables, phonemes and words than other synthetic voices. WaveNet is generally available and is offered in dozens of languages and regional variants, including confirmed entries for Arabic, Bengali (India), Czech, Danish, Dutch (Belgium and Netherlands), English (Australia, India, UK and US), Filipino, Finnish, and French (Canada and France), per Google's Voices documentation. Google introduced WaveNet in July 2018, per its Text-to-Speech release notes, and its Voice Types documentation now also offers the newer Neural2 and Chirp 3: HD premium voice types, the latter described by Google as its latest generation of speech technology.
disadvantages: WaveNet was introduced in 2018, per Google's Text-to-Speech release notes, predating the newer Neural2 and Chirp 3: HD voice types; Google's documentation describes Chirp 3: HD as its latest generation of speech technology.

sources.title: Supported voices and languages | Cloud Text-to-Speech Documentation
Chirp 3: HD voices | Cloud Text-to-Speech Documentation

use_cases: General-purpose speech synthesis needing more natural-sounding, human-like speech than other synthetic voices, per Google's Voice Types documentation.

advantages: Meta reports an AUC of 0.995 for English-language attack detection.
Meta reports 19.3 ms per-classification latency on an A100 GPU, faster than the larger 86M variant.
Uses adversarial-resistant tokenization intended to counter attacks such as whitespace manipulation, per Meta's model card.
Evaluated by Meta for attack detection across eight languages: English, French, German, Hindi, Italian, Portuguese, Spanish, and Thai.
groq/meta-llama/llama-prompt-guard-2-22m.description: Llama Prompt Guard 2 22M is a lightweight text classifier from Meta, built on the DeBERTa-xsmall architecture with 22 million parameters, that detects prompt injection and jailbreak attempts in text sent to an LLM. Given an input, it labels it as either "benign" or "malicious" rather than generating a reply. It is the smaller and faster of Meta's two Prompt Guard 2 classifiers, meant to run as a low-latency safety filter in front of another LLM rather than as a conversational model itself.
disadvantages: Meta states the model remains vulnerable to adaptive attacks.
Multilingual detection (AUC 0.942) is weaker than its English-only detection and than the larger 86M model, per Meta's model card.
Limited to 512 input tokens.
A classifier only: it outputs a benign/malicious label, not a chat completion or explanation.

use_cases: Screening user or tool inputs for prompt injection before they reach a downstream LLM.
Detecting jailbreak attempts in LLM or agent pipelines.
Low-latency safety filtering where the larger 86M classifier's latency is too high.
Monitoring production LLM traffic for misuse patterns.

advantages: Meta reports an AUC of 0.998 for English-language attack detection and 0.995 for multilingual detection.
Built on mDeBERTa-base, giving stronger multilingual attack detection than the smaller 22M model, per Meta's model card.
Uses adversarial-resistant tokenization intended to counter attacks such as whitespace manipulation, per Meta's model card.
Evaluated by Meta for attack detection across eight languages: English, French, German, Hindi, Italian, Portuguese, Spanish, and Thai.
groq/meta-llama/llama-prompt-guard-2-86m.description: Llama Prompt Guard 2 86M is Meta's larger prompt-attack classifier, built on the mDeBERTa-base architecture with 86 million parameters, that detects prompt injection and jailbreak attempts in text sent to an LLM. Given an input, it labels it as either "benign" or "malicious" rather than generating a reply. Its multilingual base model gives it stronger cross-language attack detection than Meta's smaller 22M variant, at higher latency, and it is meant to run as a safety filter in front of another LLM rather than as a conversational model itself.
disadvantages: Meta states the model remains vulnerable to adaptive attacks.
Higher latency (92.4 ms per classification on an A100 GPU) than the 22M variant, per Meta's model card.
Limited to 512 input tokens.
A classifier only: it outputs a benign/malicious label, not a chat completion or explanation.

evaluations.name: Attack Prevention Rate (real-world agentic eval, 3% utility reduction)

use_cases: Screening user or tool inputs for prompt injection before they reach a downstream LLM.
Detecting jailbreak attempts in LLM or agent pipelines, including multilingual inputs.
Complementing existing safety measures as an additional filtering layer.
Monitoring production LLM traffic for misuse patterns.

advantages: OpenAI reports gpt-oss-120b matches or exceeds OpenAI o4-mini on core reasoning benchmarks including competition coding, general problem solving and tool calling, per OpenAI's launch post.
Scores 90.0% on MMLU and 80.1% on GPQA Diamond at high reasoning effort, per OpenAI's gpt-oss model card (arXiv:2508.10925).
Scores 62.4% on SWE-bench Verified and 57.6% on HealthBench at high reasoning effort, per OpenAI's gpt-oss model card.
Fits on a single 80GB GPU using native MXFP4 quantization of the MoE weights, per OpenAI's Hugging Face model card.
Exposes full chain-of-thought reasoning for debugging and transparency, and supports adjustable reasoning effort (low, medium, high), per OpenAI's launch post.
groq/openai/gpt-oss-120b.description: gpt-oss-120b is OpenAI's larger open-weight reasoning model, released under an Apache 2.0 license in August 2025. It uses a mixture-of-experts transformer architecture with 117 billion total parameters and 5.1 billion active parameters per token, and is designed to fit on a single 80GB GPU (NVIDIA H100 or AMD MI300X) using native MXFP4 quantization of its MoE weights. The model supports low, medium and high reasoning-effort settings, exposes its full chain of thought, and is trained for agentic tool use including function calling, Python code execution and web browsing. It requires OpenAI's harmony response format to operate correctly.
disadvantages: Requires OpenAI's harmony response format; OpenAI's model card states the model will not function correctly without it.
Reported knowledge cutoff of June 2024, per OpenAI's developer documentation.
Trained mostly on English, text-only data, per OpenAI's launch post.
use_cases: Agentic workflows with function calling, Python code execution and web browsing
Production-scale reasoning and coding deployments on a single high-memory GPU
Custom fine-tuning for specialized or on-premises deployments
General-purpose chat and instruction-following with adjustable reasoning effort

advantages: OpenAI reports gpt-oss-20b matches or exceeds OpenAI o3-mini on core reasoning benchmarks including competition coding, general problem solving and tool calling, per OpenAI's launch post.
Scores 85.3% on MMLU and 71.5% on GPQA Diamond at high reasoning effort, per OpenAI's gpt-oss model card (arXiv:2508.10925).
Scores 60.7% on SWE-bench Verified and 42.5% on HealthBench at high reasoning effort, per OpenAI's gpt-oss model card.
Runs within 16GB of memory using native MXFP4 quantization of the MoE weights, enabling local and consumer-hardware deployment, per OpenAI's Hugging Face model card.
Exposes full chain-of-thought reasoning for debugging and transparency, and supports adjustable reasoning effort (low, medium, high), per OpenAI's launch post.
groq/openai/gpt-oss-20b.description: gpt-oss-20b is OpenAI's smaller open-weight reasoning model, released under an Apache 2.0 license in August 2025 alongside the larger gpt-oss-120b. It uses a mixture-of-experts transformer architecture with 21 billion total parameters and 3.6 billion active parameters per token, and is designed to run within 16GB of memory using native MXFP4 quantization of its MoE weights, suiting local or specialized deployment. The model supports low, medium and high reasoning-effort settings, exposes its full chain of thought, and is trained for agentic tool use including function calling, Python code execution and web browsing. It requires OpenAI's harmony response format to operate correctly.
disadvantages: Requires OpenAI's harmony response format; OpenAI's model card states the model will not function correctly without it.
Reported knowledge cutoff of June 2024, per OpenAI's developer documentation.
Trained mostly on English, text-only data, per OpenAI's launch post.
Scores lower than the larger gpt-oss-120b on MMLU, GPQA Diamond, SWE-bench Verified and HealthBench, per OpenAI's gpt-oss model card.
use_cases: On-device and local inference on consumer or specialized hardware
Low-latency agentic workflows with function calling, Python code execution and web browsing
Custom fine-tuning for resource-constrained deployments
General-purpose chat and instruction-following with adjustable reasoning effort

advantages: OpenAI reports that on internal multi-policy accuracy tests, gpt-oss-safeguard-20b outperforms gpt-5-thinking and the base gpt-oss models, per OpenAI's launch post.
OpenAI reports gpt-oss-safeguard slightly outperformed all other tested models on a 2022 content-moderation dataset, per OpenAI's launch post.
Exposes its reasoning process for each classification decision, making it possible to audit why content was labeled a certain way, per OpenAI's Hugging Face model card.
Interprets a custom, written policy at inference time rather than requiring retraining, so one model can generalize across products and use cases, per OpenAI's launch post.
Lower-latency alternative to gpt-oss-safeguard-120b, built on the smaller gpt-oss-20b base, per OpenAI's Hugging Face model card.
groq/openai/gpt-oss-safeguard-20b.description: gpt-oss-safeguard-20b is OpenAI's smaller open-weight reasoning model for safety classification, released as a research preview in October 2025 under an Apache 2.0 license alongside the larger gpt-oss-safeguard-120b. It is a reasoning fine-tune of gpt-oss-20b (21 billion total / 3.6 billion active parameters) that takes a user-supplied written policy and a piece of content, classifies the content against that policy, and returns its chain-of-thought reasoning alongside the decision rather than only a score. It supports low, medium and high reasoning-effort settings and, like the base gpt-oss models, requires OpenAI's harmony response format. OpenAI recommends the base gpt-oss models for non-safety use cases.
disadvantages: Released as a research preview, per OpenAI's launch post.
Performance was mixed on the ToxicChat benchmark, where gpt-5-thinking marginally outperformed gpt-oss-safeguard-20b, per OpenAI's launch post.

OpenAI notes traditional classifiers trained on large labeled datasets can still outperform gpt-oss-safeguard, and its reasoning process is more computationally expensive to run at scale, per OpenAI's launch post.
Requires OpenAI's harmony response format; OpenAI recommends the base gpt-oss models for applications outside safety classification, per OpenAI's Hugging Face model card.
use_cases: LLM input/output filtering against a custom safety policy
Online content labeling and moderation
Offline Trust and Safety labeling at scale
Lower-latency, auditable policy-based content classification

advantages: Scores 90.3% on LiveCodeBench v6 for competitive coding, per its Hugging Face model card.
Scores 89.2% on GPQA Diamond for scientific reasoning, per its Hugging Face model card.
Scores 84.3% on OSWorld-Verified for computer-use tasks and 81.9% on AndroidWorld for mobile-use tasks, per its Hugging Face model card.
Scores 91.1% on OmniDocBench 1.5 for document understanding, per its Hugging Face model card.
Supports a toggleable "thinking" reasoning mode with an adjustable reasoning_effort parameter and tool calling, per its Hugging Face model card and GitHub README.
groq/qwen/qwen3.8-27b.description: Qwen3.8-27B is a dense 27-billion-parameter multimodal model from Alibaba's Qwen team, part of the Qwen3.8 series (built on the Qwen3.5 architecture) and released in August 2026. It combines text generation with native vision-language understanding of images and documents, and supports a toggleable "thinking" reasoning mode with an adjustable reasoning_effort parameter, plus tool calling for agentic use. Qwen's own model card states a native context length of 262,144 tokens, extensible to 1,000,000 tokens; on this catalog it is listed with a 131,042-token input limit and a 16,384-token output limit.
disadvantages: Groq's model listing marks this model as a preview, "intended for evaluation purposes only and should not be used in production environments."
Released in August 2026, so it has limited independent evaluation beyond the maker's own benchmark tables.
use_cases: Agentic coding and software-engineering tasks.
Long-horizon autonomous planning and computer-use agents (browser, desktop, mobile).
Multimodal document and image understanding.
Visual math and scientific reasoning tasks.
General chat with an optional extended "thinking" mode for harder problems.

advantages: Hugging Face's Open ASR Leaderboard reports a mean word error rate of 7.44 for this model, and OpenAI's model card states a 10% to 20% reduction in errors versus Whisper large-v2.
Groq reports word error rates of 8.4% for short-form audio, 10.0% for sequential long-form audio, and 11.0% for chunked long-form audio.
Supports both transcription and translation to English, unlike the large-v3-turbo variant which supports transcription only.
OpenAI's model card describes improved robustness to accents, background noise, and technical language versus many existing ASR systems.
groq/whisper-large-v3.description: Whisper large-v3 is OpenAI's automatic speech recognition and speech translation model, a 1.55-billion-parameter transformer encoder-decoder trained on 5 million hours of audio (1 million hours of weakly labeled data plus 4 million hours of pseudo-labeled data), released in November 2023. It supports transcription across 99 languages, with OpenAI reporting strong ASR results in around 10 of them, and can also translate speech into English. Versus large-v2 it adds 128 Mel frequency bins (up from 80) and a Cantonese language token. On Groq it is served for transcription; Groq's speech-to-text docs list it as the model to use when both transcription and translation are needed.
disadvantages: Prone to hallucinating text that is not actually present in the audio, per OpenAI's model card.
Word error rates vary substantially across languages, with lower accuracy on low-resource languages.
OpenAI's model card notes word error rates differ across speakers of different genders, races, and ages.
Groq reports 189x real-time processing speed, slower than the 216x it reports for whisper-large-v3-turbo.
use_cases: Legal, medical, and academic transcription.
International conference and meeting transcription.
Transcription in challenging audio conditions with background noise or multiple speakers.
Multilingual transcription and speech translation into English.

advantages: Hugging Face's model card reports a mean word error rate of 7.83, close to large-v3's 7.44 despite an 8x reduction in decoder layers.
Groq reports a real-time processing speed factor of 216x, faster than the 189x it reports for whisper-large-v3.
Uses the same encoder as whisper-large-v3, retaining most of its multilingual transcription accuracy at a fraction of the decoding cost.
groq/whisper-large-v3-turbo.description: Whisper large-v3-turbo is OpenAI's speed-optimized speech recognition model, a pruned version of large-v3 that reduces the decoder from 32 layers to 4 while keeping the same encoder. It has 809 million parameters and supports transcription across 99 languages, trading a small amount of accuracy for substantially faster inference than large-v3. On Groq it is offered for transcription only; unlike large-v3, Groq's docs state it does not support the speech translation task.
disadvantages: Does not support the speech translation task on Groq; only transcription is available.
Slightly higher mean word error rate than whisper-large-v3 (7.83 vs 7.44, per Hugging Face's evaluation table).
Prone to hallucinating text not present in the audio, and word error rates vary across languages and demographic groups, per OpenAI's Whisper model documentation.
use_cases: Real-time applications such as live captioning, meeting transcription, and voice assistants.
High-volume batch transcription, including customer service call processing.
Cost-conscious transcription for startups and educational platforms.

advantages: Nous Research describes the model as offering 'advanced long-term context retention and multi-turn conversation capability, complex roleplaying and internal monologue abilities, and enhanced agentic function-calling.'
Supports function calling and structured JSON-mode outputs.
Uses the ChatML prompt format with system-prompt steering, which Nous Research says gives users strong control over the model's behavior.
hyperbolicai/hyperbolic/NousResearch/Her.description: Hermes 3 70B is a general-purpose chat model from Nous Research, fine-tuned from Meta's Llama 3.1 70B base model. It is built for advanced agentic function-calling, complex roleplay and internal monologue, and long multi-turn conversations, with an emphasis on letting users steer its behavior through system prompts. It uses the ChatML prompt format and is OpenAI-API compatible.
disadvantages: Nous Research states Hermes 3 performs only 'comparably' to the Llama 3.1 70B Instruct model it is fine-tuned from, with mixed strengths and weaknesses across benchmarks rather than a clear improvement.
use_cases: Agentic applications that call external tools or functions
Roleplay and creative multi-turn conversation
General-purpose chat assistants
Structured JSON output generation

advantages: Qwen reports QwQ-32B achieves performance comparable to DeepSeek-R1, a 671-billion-parameter model (37B activated), despite QwQ-32B having only 32.5B parameters, per the launch blog post.
Integrates agent-related capabilities, letting it reason while using tools and adapt its reasoning based on environmental feedback, per the launch blog post.
Released under the Apache 2.0 license on Hugging Face and ModelScope, per the launch blog post.
131,072-token context window, using YaRN scaling for prompts beyond 8,192 tokens, per the model card.
hyperbolicai/hyperbolic/Qwen/QwQ-32B.description: QwQ-32B is a 32.5-billion-parameter reasoning model from Alibaba's Qwen team, built on the Qwen2.5 architecture and released in March 2025 under the Apache 2.0 license. Unlike Qwen's conventional instruction-tuned models, QwQ is trained with supervised fine-tuning and large-scale reinforcement learning so it can think through problems before answering, and Qwen reports it reaches performance comparable to DeepSeek-R1 (a 671-billion-parameter model with 37B activated) despite its much smaller size. It also integrates agent-related capabilities, letting it reason while calling tools and adapting to feedback from its environment.
disadvantages: Requires enabling YaRN to reliably handle prompts longer than 8,192 tokens; without it, the model card reports handling of long sequences is comparatively weak.

It supports native function calling, JSON output and strong system-prompt adherence for agentic and enterprise use. Mistral AI states it performs best among open-weight models on multilingual conversations outside English and Chinese, and a dedicated reasoning variant was announced as coming soon but was not yet released at launch.
disadvantages: A dedicated reasoning version was described as 'coming soon' at launch, so this instruct release does not have a reasoning mode (Mistral AI launch post).

Multilingual conversation
Image understanding combined with text
Agentic tool use via native function calling
Production and enterprise assistants

The model is optimized for single-node inference and trained on diverse data including extensive code repositories.

Higher inference latency compared to smaller models
Commercial use requires a separate commercial license
Very long documents may still need chunking despite 128k token context window
Subject to API rate limits on La Plateforme

mistral/mistral-medium.description: Mistral Medium 3 is a state-of-the-art multimodal language model developed by Mistral AI, released in May 2025. It balances frontier-class performance with cost efficiency, offering 8X lower costs than competitors and deployment flexibility across clouds or self-hosted environments with four GPUs. The model is available via API (e.g., `mistral-medium-latest`) and supports complex reasoning and multimodal tasks.
disadvantages: Proprietary license restricts open-source flexibility
Self-hosted deployment requires environments with four GPUs or more
Older `mistral-medium` endpoint is deprecated, requiring migration to newer versions
use_cases: Complex reasoning tasks requiring advanced multimodal analysis
Enterprise applications needing cost-effective, high-performance AI solutions
Cloud or self-hosted deployments for scalable AI integration
Multimodal applications combining text and other data types

mistral/mistral-medium-2604.description: Mistral Medium 3.5 (API version 26.04) is Mistral AI's current mid-tier flagship model, a dense 128B-parameter model released as open weights under a Modified MIT license. Mistral AI's documentation dates its release April 28, 2026, and its public launch post is dated May 22, 2026. It unifies instruction-following, reasoning and coding in a single model, with a 256K-token context window, per-request configurable reasoning effort, and vision input, and is built for long-horizon agentic tasks that call multiple tools reliably. It is now the default model behind Mistral's Le Chat assistant and replaces Devstral 2 as the default in Mistral's Vibe coding agent.
disadvantages: Supersedes Mistral Medium 3 and Mistral Medium 3.1, which Mistral AI's models overview page lists as deprecated with retirement on August 31, 2026.

mistral/mistral-medium-latest.description: Mistral Medium 3 (mistral-medium-2505) is a medium-sized frontier model developed by Mistral AI, released in May 2025. It offers a balance between performance and cost, with an 8X lower cost than comparable models and a 128k token context window. The model is optimized for enterprise deployment on four GPUs or more, featuring a transformer-based dense decoder-only architecture and support for continuous pretraining, fine-tuning, and domain-specific adaptations.

mistral/mistral-moderation-2603.description: Mistral Moderation 2 (API id mistral-moderation-2603) is Mistral AI's current content-moderation classifier, offered through the Moderations API's two endpoints, one for raw text and one for the last message of a conversation. It scores each input from 0 to 1 across content categories that developers compare against their own thresholds to decide what to flag. Mistral AI's documentation lists a 128k-token context window and 11 policy categories in total -- Sexual, Hate and Discrimination, Violence and Threats, Dangerous, Criminal, Self-Harm, Health, Financial, Law, PII, and a dedicated Jailbreaking category for attempts to bypass or circumvent a model's safety guidelines through prompt manipulation -- up from the 9 categories in the original 2024 Mistral Moderation model. It is a Premier-tier, proprietary model, not released with open weights.

mistral/mistral-small.description: Mistral Small is a 24-billion-parameter multimodal large language model developed by Mistral AI, designed for tasks like programming, mathematical reasoning, document understanding, and dialogue. It features a transformer-based dense decoder-only architecture with an expanded context window of up to 128,000 tokens (versions 3.1+). The model supports both text and vision inputs, with open-source Apache 2.0 licensing and deployment flexibility across cloud platforms and consumer hardware when quantized.

mistral/mistral-small-2603.description: Mistral Small 4 (API id mistral-small-2603) is an open-weight model Mistral AI released on March 16, 2026 that it describes as consolidating the strengths of three previously separate models -- Magistral's reasoning, Devstral's agentic coding, and Mistral Small's instruction-following -- into one hybrid model. It is a mixture-of-experts model with 128 experts (4 active per token), 119B total parameters (6B active per token, 8B including embedding and output layers), a 256k-token context window, and text-plus-image input. A configurable reasoning-effort setting lets the same model give fast, low-effort answers or deeper, higher-effort reasoning on a per-request basis. It is released under the Apache 2.0 license with open weights.

advantages: Mistral reports approximately 4% word error rate on the FLEURS benchmark for this model, per its Voxtral Transcribe 2 launch post.

mistral/voxtral-mini-2602.description: Voxtral Mini Transcribe 2 (also called Voxtral Mini Transcribe V2) is Mistral AI's batch speech-to-text model, released February 4, 2026 as the successor to the original Voxtral Mini Transcribe. Mistral's docs describe it as an efficient audio input model "pre-trained and optimized for transcription purposes only," and its launch post reports approximately 4% word error rate on the FLEURS benchmark. It adds speaker diarization, context biasing for up to 100 custom words or phrases, and word-level timestamps, and handles recordings up to 3 hours long.
disadvantages: Positioned by Mistral for offline, batch transcription; Mistral offers a separate Voxtral Mini Transcribe Realtime model for live or streaming use cases, per Mistral's documentation and launch post.
Mistral documents strong performance in 13 languages; broader language coverage is not stated, per Mistral's Voxtral Transcribe 2 launch post.
use_cases: Meeting intelligence and transcription, per Mistral's Voxtral Transcribe 2 launch post.
Contact center and call center automation, per Mistral's Voxtral Transcribe 2 launch post.
Media and broadcast subtitling, enabled by word-level timestamps, per Mistral's launch post.
Compliance documentation, including GDPR- and HIPAA-compliant deployments, per Mistral's launch post.

advantages: Mistral's launch post states latency is configurable down to sub-200ms, enabling voice agents and other real-time applications.
Open-weight under the Apache 2.0 license and published on Hugging Face as Voxtral-Mini-4B-Realtime-2602, per Mistral's model card.
Uses a natively streaming architecture with causal attention in the audio encoder and sliding-window attention for continuous streaming, per Mistral's Hugging Face model card.
Mistral's model card states that at a 480ms delay it matches the performance of leading offline open-source transcription models, with throughput exceeding 12.5 tokens per second.
mistral/voxtral-mini-realtime-latest.description: Voxtral Mini Transcribe Realtime, released by Mistral AI on February 4, 2026 as an open-weight sibling to Voxtral Mini Transcribe V2, is a 4-billion-parameter streaming speech-to-text model published on Hugging Face as Voxtral-Mini-4B-Realtime-2602 under the Apache 2.0 license. Mistral describes it as purpose-built for live transcription, pairing a roughly 3.4B-parameter language model with a roughly 970M-parameter causal audio encoder to support configurable transcription delay from 80ms up to 2.4 seconds. Mistral's own Hugging Face model card reports an average FLEURS word error rate of 8.72% at a 480ms delay, versus 5.90% for the offline Voxtral Mini Transcribe V2, with per-language WER at that delay ranging from 3.31% for Spanish to 22.53% for Arabic.
disadvantages: Mistral's own Hugging Face model card reports a higher average FLEURS word error rate at a 480ms delay (8.72%) than its offline sibling Voxtral Mini Transcribe V2 (5.90%), a roughly 2.8-point accuracy trade-off for lower latency.

advantages: Clones a voice from a reference sample as short as 2-3 seconds, with no transcript of the voice prompt required (Mistral AI, "Speaking of Voxtral").
Supports zero-shot cross-lingual voice adaptation: generating speech in one language from a voice sample recorded in another while preserving the speaker's accent (Mistral AI, "Speaking of Voxtral").
Mistral reports a model latency of 70ms for a typical 10-second, 500-character input, with a real-time factor of about 9.7x (Mistral AI, "Speaking of Voxtral").

In Mistral's own human evaluation, the model was rated more natural than ElevenLabs Flash v2.5 at similar time-to-first-audio, and reached quality parity with ElevenLabs v3 in a zero-shot multilingual custom-voice setting (Mistral AI, "Speaking of Voxtral").
mistral/voxtral-mini-tts-2603.description: Voxtral TTS is Mistral AI's text-to-speech model, released March 23, 2026, aimed at voice-agent and other real-time speech applications. It generates expressive speech and clones a voice from a reference sample as short as 2-3 seconds, without needing a transcript of that voice prompt, and Mistral says it captures the source voice's accent, inflections, intonation and disfluencies. It is a lightweight 4-billion-parameter system combining a 3.4B-parameter transformer decoder, a 390M-parameter flow-matching acoustic transformer, and a 300M-parameter neural audio codec; a version with several reference voices is released as open weights on Hugging Face under a CC BY-NC 4.0 (non-commercial) license.
disadvantages: Documented for 9 languages (English, French, German, Spanish, Dutch, Portuguese, Italian, Hindi, Arabic), narrower than some competing TTS models (Mistral AI, "Speaking of Voxtral").
The naturalness and quality comparisons against ElevenLabs are Mistral's own human evaluation, not an independent third-party benchmark (Mistral AI, "Speaking of Voxtral").
The open-weights release is under a CC BY-NC 4.0 license, which restricts commercial use of the downloaded weights (Mistral AI, "Speaking of Voxtral").

disadvantages: Moonshot AI discontinued moonshot-v1-8k, along with the rest of the moonshot-v1 series, on August 31, 2026, stating it is no longer maintained or supported and recommending kimi-k3 instead.
Text-only: no image input, unlike the series' own moonshot-v1-8k-vision-preview variant.
use_cases: General-purpose text chat completions, as part of Moonshot AI's original moonshot-v1 conversational model line before its August 2026 retirement.

advantages: Added image input to Moonshot AI's moonshot-v1 line, letting the 8,192-token-context tier take image plus text input rather than text only, per Moonshot AI's own model documentation and changelog.
moonshotai/moonshot-v1-8k-vision-preview.description: moonshot-v1-8k-vision-preview was the 8,192-token-context, image-input variant of Moonshot AI's original moonshot-v1 chat-completions line, adding vision (image plus text input, text output) alongside the text-only moonshot-v1-8k model. Moonshot AI's platform changelog records launching a moonshot-v1-vision-preview model in January 2025. Moonshot AI's developer platform, now operating under the Kimi brand at platform.kimi.ai, discontinued the entire moonshot-v1 series, including this vision-preview variant, on August 31, 2026, stating it is no longer maintained or supported and directing developers to its current flagship model, kimi-k3.
disadvantages: Moonshot AI discontinued moonshot-v1-8k-vision-preview, along with the rest of the moonshot-v1 series, on August 31, 2026, stating it is no longer maintained or supported and recommending kimi-k3 instead.
Retained a 'preview' label in its model name throughout its documented lifetime, per Moonshot AI's changelog and model list.
Smaller 8,192-token context window than the series' own moonshot-v1-32k-vision-preview sibling.
use_cases: Chat completions combining image and text input, as part of Moonshot AI's original moonshot-v1 vision-preview line before its August 2026 retirement.

advantages: As the "auto-router" entry in Moonshot's list-models API, it sat alongside the 8K/32K/128K moonshot-v1 tiers, reaching up to the series' 128K-token top tier.
moonshotai/moonshot-v1-auto.description: moonshot-v1-auto was the "auto-router" chat model in Moonshot AI's original moonshot-v1 line, alongside the fixed context-length variants moonshot-v1-8k, moonshot-v1-32k and moonshot-v1-128k; it was launched in August 2024. Moonshot AI (whose developer platform now operates as Kimi) closed the moonshot-v1 series to newly registered users in July 2026 when it launched its current flagship, Kimi K3, and fully retired the series platform-wide on August 31, 2026, after which calls to moonshot-v1-auto return a 404 "model not found" error. Moonshot AI directs remaining users to migrate to kimi-k3.
disadvantages: Fully retired by Moonshot AI on August 31, 2026; API calls to this model now return a 404 "model not found" error.
Was already closed to newly registered accounts from July 2026, before the full retirement.
Text-only: Moonshot offered vision input only through separate moonshot-v1-*-vision-preview models (also retired), not this one.
Superseded by Moonshot AI's current flagship, kimi-k3, which the maker recommends migrating to.

openai/1024-x-1024/gpt-image-1.5.description: GPT Image 1.5 is OpenAI's image generation and editing model, released December 16, 2025 as an upgrade to GPT Image 1 with more precise editing, better preservation of logos and faces, improved instruction following, and stronger text rendering for dense or small text. It generates and edits images at 1024x1024, 1024x1536 or 1536x1024 pixels via low/medium/high quality tiers. As of OpenAI's own current model documentation, it is described as OpenAI's 'previous' image generation model; OpenAI's developer community announced its successor, GPT Image 2, on April 21, 2026.
disadvantages: OpenAI's own model docs now label it 'our previous image generation model' (OpenAI API model docs), after GPT Image 2 launched April 21, 2026 as what OpenAI calls its most capable image generation model yet (OpenAI developer community announcement).
IMG.LY's benchmark scored it 1.9/5 on latency (5th slowest of the models tested) and 2.9/5 on consistency/repeatability, its lowest category score.

Community testing found edits still regenerate the whole image rather than precisely preserving unmasked areas pixel-for-pixel, so logo/face preservation means close visual similarity rather than exact preservation (OpenAI developer community announcement thread).
Does not support chat completions, Realtime, Assistants, fine-tuning, embeddings, video or audio endpoints (OpenAI API model docs).

openai/chat-latest.description: chat-latest is OpenAI's rolling alias for the Instant-tier model currently used in ChatGPT's default chat experience; the underlying snapshot is updated regularly rather than being a fixed dated release. It accepts text and image input and produces text output, and supports reasoning, function calling, structured outputs and tools such as web search, file search, image generation and a code interpreter, but not the computer-use tool. advantages: Provides access to OpenAI's flagship general-purpose models, currently GPT-5.6 Sol, for defensive security work including vulnerability discovery, secure code review, detection engineering, incident response, malware analysis, and patch validation (OpenAI's Daybreak changelog entry).
As a '-latest' alias it automatically follows updates to its underlying model rather than staying pinned to one snapshot (OpenAI's Daybreak Blue model page and Daybreak guide).
OpenAI's model page lists support for code interpreter, hosted shell, apply patch, skills, computer use, MCP, and tool search.
openai/daybreak-blue-latest.description: Daybreak Blue is an OpenAI API alias, launched August 7, 2026 as part of OpenAI's Daybreak cybersecurity access program, for defensive security work such as vulnerability discovery, secure code review, detection engineering, incident response, malware analysis, and patch validation. Rather than a model with its own unique weights, it currently resolves to OpenAI's flagship GPT-5.6 Sol snapshot with safeguards calibrated for that defensive use, and the alias automatically follows updates to that underlying model over time. Using it requires an organization and project to first be approved and provisioned through the Daybreak program. It accepts text and image input and produces text output, with OpenAI's highest reasoning-effort setting.
disadvantages: Requires separate organization and project approval and provisioning through the Daybreak program before it can be used at all; access is not available by default (OpenAI's Daybreak Blue model page).
As an alias rather than a fixed model, its underlying model and behavior can change over time without a new model id (OpenAI's Daybreak guide).

advantages: OpenAI's model page lists fine-tuning as a supported feature of GPT-3.5 Turbo, letting customers train the underlying model on their own example prompts and responses.

OpenAI describes supervised fine-tuning, the technique this model supports, as well suited to classification, nuanced translation, generating content in a specific format, and correcting instruction-following failures (OpenAI's supervised fine-tuning guide).
openai/ft:gpt-3.5-turbo.description: ft:gpt-3.5-turbo is the identifier prefix OpenAI uses for chat models fine-tuned from its GPT-3.5 Turbo base model, producing ids of the form ft:gpt-3.5-turbo-0125:{org}:{suffix}:{id}. GPT-3.5 Turbo itself is a legacy model with a 16,385-token context window, a 4,096-token max output, and a September 1, 2021 knowledge cutoff; OpenAI's own model page places it in its lowest 'Intelligence' tier and recommends GPT-4o Mini in its place as of July 2024. OpenAI is winding down its fine-tuning platform: it is closed to new users, and this base model, along with fine-tuned models built on it, is scheduled to lose API access on October 23, 2026.
disadvantages: OpenAI is winding down its fine-tuning platform: it is closed to new users, though existing users can still create jobs for a limited time, and inference on already fine-tuned models continues only until the base model is deprecated (OpenAI's supervised fine-tuning guide).
OpenAI's deprecations page schedules ft-gpt-3.5-turbo for shutdown on October 23, 2026, with gpt-5.6-terra listed as the recommended replacement base model.
OpenAI's current model page places GPT-3.5 Turbo in its lowest 'Intelligence' and 'Speed' tiers among listed models, and recommends GPT-4o Mini in its place as of July 2024.
Text-only input and output with no image, audio, or video support, and a September 1, 2021 knowledge cutoff (OpenAI's GPT-3.5 Turbo model page).
use_cases: Continued inference on chat models already fine-tuned from GPT-3.5 Turbo before OpenAI closed the fine-tuning platform to new users.
Supervised fine-tuning for classification tasks.
Supervised fine-tuning for nuanced translation.

openai/ft:gpt-3.5-turbo-0125.description: ft:gpt-3.5-turbo-0125 is the identifier prefix for chat models fine-tuned from the gpt-3.5-turbo-0125 snapshot of OpenAI's GPT-3.5 Turbo, producing ids of the form ft:gpt-3.5-turbo-0125:{org}:{suffix}:{id}. This snapshot is the model that OpenAI's plain 'gpt-3.5-turbo' alias currently points to, and OpenAI's GPT-3.5 Turbo model page already lists gpt-3.5-turbo-0125 itself as 'Deprecated' in its snapshots list; the model has a 16,385-token context window, a 4,096-token max output, and a September 1, 2021 knowledge cutoff. openai/gpt-transcribe.description: gpt-transcribe is OpenAI's speech-to-text model for transcribing completed audio files through the Transcription endpoint. OpenAI positions it as the current recommended model for general file transcription, ahead of the older whisper-1 model, which OpenAI now reserves for cases needing word-level timestamps, translation, or subtitle generation. It accepts optional prompt, keyword, and language-hint parameters to improve accuracy on domain-specific terms, multilingual audio, and code-switching, and can stream back partial transcript text as a file is processed. It does not perform speaker diarization; OpenAI directs that need to a separate gpt-4o-transcribe-diarize model.
disadvantages: Does not support speaker diarization; OpenAI directs that use case to the separate gpt-4o-transcribe-diarize model.

openai/high/1024-x-1024/gpt-image-1.5.description: GPT Image 1.5 is OpenAI's image generation and editing model, released December 16, 2025 as an upgrade to GPT Image 1 with more precise editing, better preservation of logos and faces, improved instruction following, and stronger text rendering for dense or small text. It generates and edits images at 1024x1024, 1024x1536 or 1536x1024 pixels via low/medium/high quality tiers. As of OpenAI's own current model documentation, it is described as OpenAI's 'previous' image generation model; OpenAI's developer community announced its successor, GPT Image 2, on April 21, 2026.
disadvantages: OpenAI's own model docs now label it 'our previous image generation model' (OpenAI API model docs), after GPT Image 2 launched April 21, 2026 as what OpenAI calls its most capable image generation model yet (OpenAI developer community announcement).
IMG.LY's benchmark scored it 1.9/5 on latency (5th slowest of the models tested) and 2.9/5 on consistency/repeatability, its lowest category score.

Community testing found edits still regenerate the whole image rather than precisely preserving unmasked areas pixel-for-pixel, so logo/face preservation means close visual similarity rather than exact preservation (OpenAI developer community announcement thread).
Does not support chat completions, Realtime, Assistants, fine-tuning, embeddings, video or audio endpoints (OpenAI API model docs).

It supports vision capabilities, structured JSON outputs, and function calling for external API integration.
disadvantages: Higher latency compared to GPT-4o due to extended reasoning processes

openai/o1-preview.description: OpenAI o1-preview is an advanced AI model designed for complex reasoning in science, coding, and mathematics. Beta phase limitations: no image/web support, file uploads, code interpreter, or streaming capabilities.
Strict API rate limits (20 RPM for qualified developers) and weekly message caps (50 queries/week).
Not ideal for tasks prioritizing speed or requiring multimodal input/output.

openai/o4-mini.description: OpenAI o4-mini is a cost-efficient, smaller model optimized for fast reasoning in math, coding, and visual tasks. openai/standard/1024-x-1024/gpt-image-1..description: GPT Image 1.5 is OpenAI's image generation and editing model, released December 16, 2025 as an upgrade to GPT Image 1 with more precise editing, better preservation of logos and faces, improved instruction following, and stronger text rendering for dense or small text. It generates and edits images at 1024x1024, 1024x1536 or 1536x1024 pixels via low/medium/high quality tiers. As of OpenAI's own current model documentation, it is described as OpenAI's 'previous' image generation model; OpenAI's developer community announced its successor, GPT Image 2, on April 21, 2026.
disadvantages: OpenAI's own model docs now label it 'our previous image generation model' (OpenAI API model docs), after GPT Image 2 launched April 21, 2026 as what OpenAI calls its most capable image generation model yet (OpenAI developer community announcement).
IMG.LY's benchmark scored it 1.9/5 on latency (5th slowest of the models tested) and 2.9/5 on consistency/repeatability, its lowest category score.

Community testing found edits still regenerate the whole image rather than precisely preserving unmasked areas pixel-for-pixel, so logo/face preservation means close visual similarity rather than exact preservation (OpenAI developer community announcement thread).
Does not support chat completions, Realtime, Assistants, fine-tuning, embeddings, video or audio endpoints (OpenAI API model docs).

openai/text-embedding-3-large.description: Text-embedding-3-large is OpenAI's best-performing text embedding model, designed to convert text into high-dimensional vectors for semantic analysis. It offers 3,072 default dimensions with flexible size adjustment, supports up to 8,191 tokens via the cl100k_base tokenizer, and features improved multilingual capabilities. The model excels in semantic search, clustering, classification, and cross-lingual retrieval tasks.
disadvantages: Maximum input limit of 8,191 tokens
No fine-tuning capability available
Performance degrades with very small dimensions (<256)
Requires vector database infrastructure for large-scale applications
Deterministic output (no variability in embeddings for identical inputs)
Not optimized for keyword-based matching tasks
Higher cost per token ($0.00013/1K) compared to text-embedding-3-small
use_cases: Multilingual semantic search and document retrieval
Cross-lingual content recommendation systems
Text clustering and duplicate detection
Legal document discovery and FAQ matching
Content moderation through semantic similarity
Machine learning feature engineering for text data
Personalized content recommendation across languages

advantages: 5x cheaper than text-embedding-ada-002 ($0.00002 per 1K tokens)
Outperforms ada-002 on MIRACL (44.0% vs 31.4%) and MTEB (62.3% vs 61.0%) benchmarks
Supports flexible dimensionality reduction (512-1536) without retraining
Maintains 93-100% performance across dimension reductions
Improved multilingual capabilities compared to previous models
Faster processing with lower memory footprint than large models
openai/text-embedding-3-small.description: Text-embedding-3-small is OpenAI's cost-effective text embedding model that outperforms text-embedding-ada-002 on most benchmarks while being 5x cheaper. It provides 1,536-dimensional normalized vector embeddings (with flexible dimensionality reduction) and supports up to 8,191 tokens using the cl100k_base tokenizer. The model excels in semantic search, document clustering, classification, and content deduplication tasks.
disadvantages: Maximum input limit of 8,191 tokens
Slightly lower accuracy than text-embedding-3-large (2.3% difference on MTEB)
Performance degrades with extreme dimension reduction (88% at 256 dimensions)
Not ideal for highly specialized domains requiring domain-specific fine-tuning
Fixed model architecture with no fine-tuning options
use_cases: High-volume semantic search systems
E-commerce product similarity matching
Social media content recommendation
Email categorization and spam detection
Budget-constrained academic research
Real-time chatbot semantic matching
Cross-lingual document clustering
Content deduplication in large corpora

openai/text-embedding-ada-002.description: Text-embedding-ada-002 is a transformer-based embedding model developed by OpenAI, released in December 2022. It generates 1,536-dimensional unit-length vectors using the cl100k_base tokenizer, with a maximum input of 8,191 tokens. While superseded by the text-embedding-3 series, it remains supported for legacy systems and applications requiring fixed-dimension embeddings.
disadvantages: Fixed 1,536-dimensional output with no flexibility for reduction
Higher cost compared to newer models (5x more expensive than text-embedding-3-small)
Lower multilingual performance relative to updated models
No recent training data updates since December 2022
MIRACL score of 31.4% indicates weaker cross-lingual retrieval capabilities
use_cases: Legacy systems requiring stable, fixed-dimension embeddings
Document clustering and semantic search in production environments
Chatbot memory and conversation retrieval systems
Knowledge base organization and information retrieval pipelines
Recommendation engines with pre-existing vector database integrations

advantages: Accepts requests of up to 8,192 tokens, versus 2,046 tokens for version 1 of the same model, per Microsoft's Azure OpenAI documentation.
Produces 1,536-dimension text embeddings usable with the Embeddings API, per OpenAI's model documentation and Microsoft's Azure OpenAI documentation.
Microsoft's Azure OpenAI documentation notes there is no in-place upgrade path between embedding models; moving to a newer model such as text-embedding-3-large requires regenerating embeddings.
openai/text-embedding-ada-002-v2.description: text-embedding-ada-002-v2 is version 2 of OpenAI's text-embedding-ada-002 model, which converts text into a 1,536-dimension numerical vector for measuring semantic relatedness between pieces of text. Microsoft's Azure OpenAI documentation distinguishes this version from version 1 of the same model by its larger 8,192-token maximum request size, versus 2,046 tokens for version 1. OpenAI's own model documentation labels the underlying text-embedding-ada-002 model an "Older embedding model," superseded by the third-generation text-embedding-3-small and text-embedding-3-large models.
disadvantages: OpenAI's own model page labels the underlying text-embedding-ada-002 model an "Older embedding model."
Scores lower on both MTEB (61.0 vs. 62.3/64.6) and MIRACL (31.4 vs. 44.0/54.9) than text-embedding-3-small/large, per OpenAI's reported testing as published in Microsoft's Azure OpenAI documentation.
Can only be used with Embedding API requests, not chat completions or other endpoints, per OpenAI's model documentation.

openai/tts-1.description: TTS-1 is OpenAI's standard text-to-speech model that converts written text into natural-sounding audio. It offers multiple pre-built voice options, adjustable speech rate, and supports various audio formats. The model prioritizes speed over quality for real-time applications and includes features like streaming support and voice steering for tone/style adjustments.
disadvantages: Lower audio quality compared to TTS-1-HD model
Limited to preset voices with no custom voice cloning capabilities
No fine-grained prosody control or SSML markup support
Potential artifacts in complex pronunciations and voice consistency variations
Voice selection is restricted to OpenAI's predefined options
No support for advanced text formatting or markup languages

openai/tts-1-1106.description: tts-1-1106 is OpenAI's November 6, 2023 dated snapshot of tts-1, a text-to-speech model that converts text into natural-sounding spoken audio and is optimized for real-time use cases. OpenAI describes tts-1 as trading quality for lower latency compared to its tts-1-hd sibling. It offers nine built-in voices (alloy, ash, coral, echo, fable, onyx, nova, sage, and shimmer) that OpenAI notes are currently optimized for English, and OpenAI's own documentation states the underlying model covers the same language range as its Whisper speech models. OpenAI's current guides now point developers toward the newer gpt-4o-mini-tts model for real-time applications needing more reliability and voice-style control.
disadvantages: OpenAI states tts-1 produces lower audio quality than the tts-1-hd model.
Voices are, per OpenAI's own documentation, currently optimized for English even though the model can generate speech in other languages.
OpenAI's current guidance recommends the newer gpt-4o-mini-tts model instead for real-time applications needing more reliability and voice-style control.

openai/whisper-1.description: Whisper-1 is a general-purpose speech recognition model developed by OpenAI, based on the large-v2 version of the open-source Whisper model. It supports multilingual transcription and translation, automatic language detection, and robust performance with 50% fewer errors than specialized models. The model uses an encoder-decoder Transformer architecture and is trained on 680,000 hours of multilingual data, approaching human-level robustness on English speech.
disadvantages: 25 MB file size limit per request
No real-time streaming support (requires separate Realtime API)
Struggles with heavy accents, background noise, or non-standard speech patterns
Translation output is limited to English only
Processing time increases linearly with audio length

advantages: Rev reports 9.68% WER on Earnings21, 13.68% on Earnings22, and 10.30% on Rev16, ahead of Whisper Large-v3 (14.26%, 19.05%, 10.86%) and Canary-1B (14.40%, 19.01%, 13.82%) on the same test sets.

revai/reverb.description: Reverb is Rev AI's automatic speech recognition model for English audio, built by Rev (Rev.com), a speech-to-text and captioning company. It was trained on 200,000 hours of human-transcribed audio and offers a tunable verbatimicity setting that lets users choose between a clean, readable transcript and a fully verbatim one, and pairs with Rev's own Reverb Diarization models for speaker separation. Rev has open-sourced the inference and evaluation code for Reverb on GitHub, with model weights published on Hugging Face under a separate model license, and also sells a separate Reverb Foreign Language product for non-English audio.
disadvantages: Limited to English audio; non-English transcription requires Rev AI's separate Reverb Foreign Language model.

advantages: The largest Whisper checkpoint; OpenAI's README describes the six sizes as offering "speed and accuracy tradeoffs," with large positioned as the most accurate, at the cost of speed (about 10 GB VRAM, the slowest of the family).
Deepgram pairs Whisper Cloud with diarization and word timings, which Deepgram says are not available through OpenAI's own API.
Trained on 680,000 hours of audio covering 98 languages per OpenAI's model card, giving it broad multilingual coverage.
revai/whisper-large.description: Whisper Large (1550M parameters) is the biggest and, per OpenAI's README, most accurate checkpoint in OpenAI's open-source Whisper family of speech recognition models, trained on 680,000 hours of multilingual, multitask audio and able to transcribe speech and translate it into English. It is offered as a multilingual-only checkpoint (no English-only variant). Deepgram hosts it as part of its "Whisper Cloud" offering, where model=whisper-large defaults to OpenAI's Whisper large-v2, layering diarization and word timings on top of the open model for pre-recorded audio. Rev AI separately offers a hosted "Whisper Large Transcription" option, limited to English.
disadvantages: Deepgram does not support live streaming with Whisper Cloud; only pre-recorded audio up to 20 minutes of processing time is supported.

Deepgram calls its Whisper models "less scalable than all other Deepgram models" and caps Whisper requests at 15 concurrent calls on paid plans (5 on pay-as-you-go), recommending a Deepgram model such as Nova instead if it meets the need.
The slowest of the Whisper sizes per OpenAI's README, at roughly 1x relative inference speed versus up to about 10x for the tiny checkpoint.
Deepgram's Whisper Cloud defaults whisper-large to OpenAI's Whisper large-v2 rather than a newer large checkpoint.
Rev AI's hosted Whisper Large Transcription option supports English only, unlike Rev AI's own Reverb offering which covers Spanish, French, Chinese, Portuguese and more.
OpenAI's model card reports the Whisper family is prone to hallucination and shows disparate performance across accents and dialects.

sagemaker/meta-textgeneration-llama-2-13.description: Llama 2 13B is the base, 13-billion-parameter pretrained model in Meta's Llama 2 family of auto-regressive transformer language models, trained on 2 trillion tokens of publicly available text between January and July 2023 with a pretraining data cutoff of September 2022, per Meta's model card. As a pretrained (non-chat) model it performs text completion on a prompt and can be adapted to a variety of natural language generation tasks, in contrast to the fine-tuned '-f' chat variant built for dialogue. Meta's Hugging Face organization now lists Llama 2 in a legacy 'History' section behind the current Llama 3.1, 3.2, 3.3 and 4 families.
disadvantages: Base pretrained model only, not instruction- or chat-tuned; Meta positions the fine-tuned '-f' chat variant for assistant-like dialogue.
Meta states intended use is commercial and research use in English, and that safety testing 'has not covered, nor could it cover, all scenarios.'
Superseded by later Llama generations: Meta's Hugging Face organization lists Llama 2 in a legacy 'History' section behind Llama 3.1, 3.2, 3.3 and 4.

speechmatics/batch-enhanced.description: Enhanced is Speechmatics' highest-accuracy operating point for its Batch and Realtime speech-to-text API, selected by setting the request's model field to "enhanced". It transcribes a chosen language, or auto-detects one, and carries Speechmatics' full transcription feature set. Speechmatics also offers a medical-domain variant of Enhanced, tuned for healthcare terminology and selected via a domain parameter.

speechmatics/batch-melia-1.description: Melia 1 is Speechmatics' multilingual speech-to-text model, offered for Batch transcription in the EU and US regions by setting the request's model field to "melia-1" with language set to "multi". Instead of requiring a language to be selected up front, it automatically detects the spoken language from 55 languages, handles code-switching mid-sentence, and labels each word in the output with the language it was spoken in. Speechmatics states Melia 1's accuracy matches its Standard model. As of Speechmatics' current documentation, Melia 1 does not yet support the custom vocabulary, confidence scores, speaker identification, or speech-intelligence add-ons (translation, summarization, etc.) that Speechmatics' Enhanced and Standard models offer.
disadvantages: Does not currently support custom vocabulary, confidence scores, speaker identification, or Speechmatics' speech-intelligence add-ons (translation, summarization, topic detection, chapters, sentiment analysis, audio events), which Enhanced and Standard both offer.

Speechmatics' Models documentation describes Melia 1 as an early-access model whose feature support is still expanding.
use_cases: Transcribing multilingual audio with mid-sentence code-switching
Multilingual meeting, call and media transcription where the spoken language is not known in advance
Localized transcript output using per-language word delimiters and writing direction

advantages: Speechmatics documents Standard as its fastest-turnaround operating point for Batch and Realtime transcription, per Speechmatics' Models documentation.
Speechmatics states Standard's accuracy matches its Melia 1 model, per Speechmatics' Models documentation.
Supports custom dictionaries, per-word confidence scores, and speaker diarization, the same feature set as Enhanced, per Speechmatics' Models documentation.

Bundles speech-intelligence add-ons in the same job, including translation, summarization, topic detection, chapters, sentiment analysis and audio-event detection, per Speechmatics' Models documentation.
speechmatics/batch-standard.description: Standard is Speechmatics' fastest-turnaround operating point for its Batch and Realtime speech-to-text API, selected by setting the request's model field to "standard". Speechmatics states its accuracy matches its newer Melia 1 model and sits slightly below its own Enhanced operating point, while offering the same core transcription feature set as Enhanced. Speechmatics positions Standard as the choice when throughput matters more than peak accuracy.
disadvantages: Speechmatics documents Enhanced, not Standard, as its highest-accuracy operating point, describing Standard as prioritising throughput over maximum accuracy.
use_cases: Archival transcription
Content indexing
Large-scale or bulk captioning
High-volume batch transcription where turnaround speed matters more than peak accuracy

advantages: Returns speaker-attributed, punctuated transcript segments with explicit turn-start and turn-end signals rather than a raw word stream, formatted to pass directly to an LLM, per Speechmatics' Agent STT documentation.
Speechmatics states end-of-speech finalization lands in about 350ms, per Speechmatics' Voice Agents page.
Includes speaker diarization by default, attributing every word to the speaker who said it, per Speechmatics' Voice Agents page.
Supports a custom vocabulary of up to 1,000 domain-specific terms, per Speechmatics' Voice Agents page.
Speechmatics states Agent STT is available in 55+ languages, per Speechmatics' Voice Agents page.
Integrates directly with the Vapi, LiveKit and Pipecat voice-agent platforms, plus a Python SDK and a direct WebSocket API for any other language, per Speechmatics' Agent STT documentation.
speechmatics/linden-1.description: Linden 1 is Speechmatics' speech-to-text model built specifically for Agent STT, its turn-based transcription service for voice agents, reached over a dedicated /v2/agent WebSocket endpoint; Speechmatics states Agent STT is powered by linden-1 and offers no alternative model. Rather than a running word stream, it returns speaker-attributed, punctuated segments together with explicit start-of-turn and end-of-turn signals, formatted to pass directly to an LLM. Speechmatics states Agent STT is available in 55+ languages and, as of its current documentation, on SaaS only.
disadvantages: Agent STT, the product linden-1 powers, is available on SaaS only, per Speechmatics' Agent STT documentation.
Linden 1 is the only model Agent STT offers, so there is no alternative model to choose for this endpoint.
